subject: science
name: Sound Waves
summary: Sound is produced by vibrating objects and travels through a medium as a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions. A sound wave is described by its wavelength, frequency, time period, amplitude and speed (v = λν). Sound travels fastest in solids, has loudness, pitch and quality, reflects to give echoes and reverberation, and beyond the human range we find infrasound and ultrasound, used in SONAR, medical scans and by animals like bats.

topics.title: How sound is produced and why it needs a medium
topics.summary: Every sound comes from something vibrating. Sound needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel, so it cannot travel through a vacuum — as the bell-jar experiment shows.
topics.simple: Every sound you hear comes from something **vibrating** — moving quickly back and forth. Touch your throat while humming and you can feel your vocal cords vibrate. Sound also needs something to travel through, like air, water or a wall. In empty space (a vacuum) there is nothing to carry it, so there is no sound.
topics.explain:
**Sound is produced by vibration.** A vibrating object moves rapidly to and fro about its resting position and disturbs the medium around it.
- **Tuning fork:** strike it on a rubber pad and its prongs vibrate. Touch a prong to water and it splashes; touch it to a hanging table-tennis ball and the ball is pushed away.
- **Human voice:** air from the lungs makes the **vocal cords** in the larynx (voice box) vibrate.
- Other examples: the stretched skin of a tabla or dholak, the strings of a sitar or veena, the air column in a flute or shehnai.

**Sound needs a medium.** The substance through which sound travels — solid, liquid or gas — is called the **medium**.

**Bell-jar experiment:**
1. Place an electric bell inside an airtight glass bell jar connected to a vacuum pump.
2. Switch on the bell — you can hear it ringing.
3. Slowly pump the air out of the jar.
4. The sound becomes **fainter and fainter**, even though you can still see the hammer striking the bell.
5. With almost all the air removed, you can hardly hear anything.

**Conclusion:** sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it needs a material medium. Light, on the other hand, can travel through a vacuum — that's why you can still see the bell.
topics.example: Astronauts on a spacewalk can't talk to each other directly, even if they are close, because space is almost a vacuum. They use radio, which works through a vacuum. But if two astronauts touch helmets, they can hear each other faintly — the sound travels through the solid helmets.
keyPoints: All sound is produced by vibrating objects
Human voice: vibration of vocal cords in the larynx
Sound needs a material medium — solid, liquid or gas
Bell-jar: sound fades as air is pumped out
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum; light can

topics.title: Propagation of sound: compressions and rarefactions
topics.summary: Sound travels as a longitudinal wave: particles of the medium vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, forming compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure). Energy moves forward; the medium does not.
topics.simple: When a tuning fork prong pushes forward, it squeezes the air in front — a **compression**. When it moves back, it leaves a thinned-out region — a **rarefaction**. These squeezes and stretches pass along the air like a push passing down a queue of people. Each air particle only wiggles back and forth; it's the **energy** that travels to your ear.
topics.explain:
**How the disturbance travels:**
- A vibrating object pushes the air particles next to it, which push their neighbours, and so on.
- Each particle **vibrates about its own position** and passes the disturbance on. The particles do **not** travel from the source to your ear.
- What travels is **energy** — the wave carries energy without carrying the medium along.

**Compressions and rarefactions:**
- **Compression (C):** a region where particles are crowded together — **high density and high pressure**.
- **Rarefaction (R):** a region where particles are spread apart — **low density and low pressure**.
- As the source vibrates, it creates a series of compressions and rarefactions that move outwards.

**Longitudinal wave:** a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate **parallel** to (back and forth along) the direction in which the wave travels. Sound in air is a longitudinal wave.

Compare this with a **transverse wave**, where particles move **perpendicular** to the wave's direction — like ripples on water or a wave on a shaken rope.

A stretched **slinky** shows both: push and pull one end along its length and you see compressions and rarefactions travel along it (longitudinal); shake it sideways and you get a transverse wave.
topics.example: Picture people standing in a queue at a railway ticket counter. If someone at the back gives a gentle push, it passes person to person to the front. Nobody leaves their place in the line — only the push travels. Sound moves through air the same way.
keyPoints: Sound travels as compressions and rarefactions
Compression = high pressure/density; rarefaction = low pressure/density
Particles vibrate about their mean position; they don't travel along
The wave carries energy, not matter
Sound is a longitudinal wave: vibration parallel to direction of travel
Transverse wave: vibration perpendicular to direction of travel

topics.title: Characteristics of a sound wave: λ, ν, T, amplitude and v = λν
topics.summary: Wavelength (λ) is the distance between two consecutive compressions; frequency (ν) is the number of oscillations per second (Hz); time period T = 1/ν; amplitude is the maximum disturbance; speed v = λν.
topics.simple: A sound wave can be described by a few numbers. **Wavelength** is the length of one complete wave. **Frequency** is how many waves pass each second, measured in hertz (Hz). **Time period** is the time for one wave. **Amplitude** is how big the disturbance is. And the **speed** of sound is wavelength × frequency.
topics.explain:
A sound wave can be drawn as a graph of density (or pressure) against distance: compressions are the **crests** (peaks) and rarefactions are the **troughs** (valleys).

- **Wavelength (λ, lambda):** the distance between two consecutive compressions (or two consecutive rarefactions). SI unit: **metre (m)**.
- **Frequency (ν, nu):** the number of complete oscillations (compressions passing a point) per second. SI unit: **hertz (Hz)**; 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second. The frequency of a sound is the same as the frequency of the source that made it.
- **Time period (T):** the time taken for one complete oscillation. SI unit: **second (s)**.
- **Relation:** **ν = 1/T** (and T = 1/ν).
- **Amplitude (A):** the maximum disturbance of the medium on either side of its normal (mean) value. A bigger amplitude means the wave carries more energy.
- **Intensity:** the amount of sound energy passing each second through a unit area. It depends on amplitude.

**Speed of sound (v):** the distance a compression travels per unit time. In one time period T, the wave moves one wavelength λ, so

v = λ / T = **λν**

This is called the **wave equation**. For a given medium (at a given temperature), the speed is fixed, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
topics.example:
**Example 1:** A sound wave has a time period of 0.005 s. Find its frequency.
ν = 1/T = 1/0.005 = **200 Hz**

**Example 2:** A sound of frequency 173 Hz travels in air at 346 m/s. Find its wavelength.
λ = v/ν = 346/173 = **2 m**

**Example 3:** A sound wave in water has wavelength 1.5 m and frequency 1000 Hz. Find its speed.
v = λν = 1.5 × 1000 = **1500 m/s**
keyPoints: Wavelength λ = distance between two consecutive compressions (m)
Frequency ν = oscillations per second (Hz)
Time period T = time for one oscillation (s); ν = 1/T
Amplitude = maximum disturbance; bigger amplitude → more energy
Intensity = sound energy per second per unit area
Wave equation: v = λν

topics.title: Speed of sound in different media
topics.summary: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases (air ≈ 346 m/s at 25 °C, steel ≈ 5960 m/s). Its speed also increases with temperature.
topics.simple: Sound moves at different speeds in different materials. It is fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases. In air at room temperature it goes about 346 m/s, but in steel it zooms at nearly 6000 m/s. Sound also travels a little faster when the air is warmer.
topics.explain:
The speed of sound depends on the **medium** and its **temperature**.

**Speed of sound at 25 °C:**
- Aluminium — 6420 m/s
- Steel — 5960 m/s
- Glass — 3980 m/s
- Sea water — 1531 m/s
- Distilled water — 1498 m/s
- Hydrogen — 1284 m/s
- Air — 346 m/s

**Patterns:**
- **Solids > liquids > gases** in general. Particles in solids are closely packed and strongly linked, so the disturbance passes on quickly.
- Sound is slightly faster in sea water than in distilled water.
- Among gases, it is much faster in light hydrogen than in air.
- **Temperature:** the speed of sound **increases** as temperature rises. In air it is about 331 m/s at 0 °C and 346 m/s at 25 °C.

**Sound vs light:** light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s, nearly a million times faster than sound in air. That is why we see a lightning flash before we hear the thunder, and see a cricket ball being hit before we hear the 'tock' from far away in the stands.
topics.example:
During a monsoon storm, you see lightning and hear the thunder 3 s later. The light reaches you almost instantly, so the distance to the lightning is about

distance = speed × time = 346 m/s × 3 s = **1038 m** (about 1 km).
keyPoints: Speed order: solids > liquids > gases
At 25 °C: aluminium 6420, steel 5960, glass 3980 m/s
Sea water 1531, distilled water 1498, hydrogen 1284, air 346 m/s
Speed of sound increases with temperature
Light is far faster than sound — lightning seen before thunder heard

topics.title: Loudness, pitch, quality and the audible range
topics.summary: Loudness depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels (dB); pitch depends on frequency; quality (timbre) lets us tell apart sounds of the same pitch and loudness. Humans hear 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
topics.simple: Hit a drum hard and the sound is **loud** (big vibrations, big amplitude); tap it gently and it is soft. A whistle sounds **high-pitched** because it vibrates many times a second (high frequency); a lion's roar is low-pitched. **Quality** is what lets you tell a flute from a violin even when they play the same note equally loudly. Our ears can hear from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
topics.explain:
**Loudness**
- How strong a sound seems to our ears.
- Depends on **amplitude**: larger amplitude → more energy → louder sound.
- Measured in **decibels (dB)**. A whisper is about 30 dB and normal conversation about 60 dB; long exposure to very loud sounds (roughly 85 dB and above) can damage hearing.
- Loudness is how our ear *feels* the sound; **intensity** is the actual energy per second per unit area. Two sounds of equal intensity may not seem equally loud, because the ear is more sensitive to some frequencies than others.

**Pitch**
- How high or low (shrill or deep) a sound seems.
- Depends on **frequency**: higher frequency → higher pitch.
- A child's or woman's voice usually has a higher pitch than a man's; a bird's chirp is high-pitched; a lion's roar is low-pitched.

**Quality (timbre)**
- The feature that lets us tell apart two sounds of the **same pitch and loudness** — e.g. a flute and a harmonium playing the same note, or recognising a friend's voice on the phone.
- It depends on the **shape of the wave** (the mix of frequencies the source produces).

**Audible range**
Humans can hear sounds of frequency from about **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)**. Below 20 Hz is **infrasound**; above 20 kHz is **ultrasound**.
topics.example: On a harmonium, the keys on the right give higher notes: they make the reeds vibrate at a higher frequency, so the pitch is higher. Pressing the bellows harder doesn't change the pitch — it makes the reeds vibrate with larger amplitude, so the sound is louder.
keyPoints: Loudness depends on amplitude; unit: decibel (dB)
Pitch depends on frequency — higher frequency, higher pitch
Quality (timbre) distinguishes sounds of the same pitch and loudness
Quality depends on the waveform
Audible range: 20 Hz – 20 kHz
Below 20 Hz = infrasound; above 20 kHz = ultrasound

topics.title: Reflection of sound, echo and reverberation
topics.summary: Sound reflects from hard surfaces following the laws of reflection. An echo is heard only if the reflected sound arrives at least 0.1 s later, needing a reflector at least about 17 m away. Reverberation is the persistence of sound from repeated reflections.
topics.simple: Sound bounces off walls, cliffs and buildings just like a ball bounces off a wall. If you shout at a cliff far enough away, you hear your voice come back — an **echo**. Your brain can only tell the echo apart if it arrives at least 0.1 s later, so the cliff must be at least about 17 m away. In a big empty hall, sound bounces around many times and lingers — that's **reverberation**.
topics.explain:
**Laws of reflection of sound** (same as for light):
1. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
2. The incident sound, the reflected sound and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
Sound reflects best from large, hard, polished or rough surfaces (walls, cliffs, buildings).

**Echo:** the sound heard after reflection from a distant surface.
- The sensation of a sound stays in our brain for about **0.1 s**. So the echo is heard separately only if it returns **at least 0.1 s** after the original sound.
- **Minimum distance for an echo** (air at 25 °C, v = 346 m/s):
  total distance travelled = v × t = 346 × 0.1 = 34.6 m (there and back)
  distance to reflector = 34.6 ÷ 2 ≈ **17.3 m — about 17 m**
- This minimum distance becomes a little smaller in hot weather, when sound travels faster.
- Rolling of thunder is due to repeated reflections from clouds and the ground.

**Reverberation:** the persistence (lingering) of sound in a large hall due to **repeated reflections** from walls, ceiling and floor. Too much reverberation makes speech and music blurred.
**Reducing reverberation:** cover the walls and ceiling with **sound-absorbing materials** — fibreboard, rough plaster, heavy curtains, carpets, and use seats with soft, cushioned material.

**Uses of multiple reflection of sound:**
- **Megaphone, loudhailer, horns, shehnai, trumpet:** the tube and cone-shaped opening reflect sound again and again so it goes forward towards the listeners instead of spreading out.
- **Stethoscope:** the doctor hears the heartbeat because sound undergoes multiple reflections along the tube.
- **Curved ceilings** of halls and auditoriums reflect sound evenly to all parts of the hall.
- **Sound board:** a curved board placed behind the stage (speaker at its focus) reflects sound evenly towards the audience.
topics.example:
**Echo distance:** A student claps near a hillside and hears the echo 2 s later. Speed of sound in air = 346 m/s.

Total distance (to the hill and back) = 346 × 2 = 692 m
Distance to hill = 692 ÷ 2 = **346 m**

We divide by 2 because the sound travels to the hill and back.
keyPoints: Laws of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection; all in one plane
Echo needs a gap of at least 0.1 s
Minimum echo distance = 346 × 0.1 ÷ 2 ≈ 17 m
Reverberation = persistence of sound by repeated reflections
Reduce reverberation with curtains, carpets, fibreboard, rough plaster, cushioned seats
Uses: megaphone, stethoscope, sound board, curved ceilings

topics.title: Infrasound, ultrasound and SONAR
topics.summary: Infrasound (< 20 Hz) is made by elephants, whales and earthquakes; ultrasound (> 20 kHz) is used by bats and dolphins and heard by dogs. Ultrasound is used for cleaning, ultrasonography, detecting flaws in metals and in SONAR (depth = speed × time ÷ 2).
topics.simple: Some sounds are too low (below 20 Hz) or too high (above 20,000 Hz) for us to hear. The very low ones are **infrasound** — elephants and whales use them, and earthquakes make them. The very high ones are **ultrasound** — bats use them to 'see' in the dark and dogs can hear them. Ultrasound helps doctors see babies before birth and helps ships measure how deep the sea is.
topics.explain:
**Infrasound** (frequency **below 20 Hz**):
- Produced by **elephants** and **whales** (used to communicate over long distances)
- Produced by **earthquakes** before the main shock waves; some animals may sense it and become restless
- A vibrating simple pendulum also produces infrasound

**Ultrasound** (frequency **above 20 kHz**):
- Produced by **bats**, **dolphins** and porpoises
- **Dogs** can hear ultrasound — that's how a 'silent' dog whistle works
- Ultrasound can travel along well-defined straight paths even when there are obstacles

**Uses of ultrasound:**
- **Cleaning** hard-to-reach parts — spiral tubes, odd-shaped parts, electronic components: the object is put in a cleaning liquid and ultrasound shakes the dirt and grease loose.
- **Detecting flaws (cracks) in metal** blocks and structures: ultrasound passes through the metal but is reflected back by a crack or hole, revealing the flaw.
- **Ultrasonography (medical imaging):** echoes of ultrasound from organs such as the liver, gall bladder, uterus and kidneys are turned into images. It is used to check the growth of a baby during pregnancy.

**Echolocation in bats:** a bat flying in the dark emits high-pitched ultrasonic squeaks. The waves reflect from obstacles or insects and return to the bat's ears. From the echoes, the bat judges where the object is and how far away.

**SONAR** (Sound Navigation And Ranging): a ship has a **transmitter** that sends ultrasound into the water and a **detector** that receives the echo from the sea bed (or a submarine, shipwreck or iceberg). If the echo returns after time t and the speed of sound in sea water is v, the sound has travelled to the bottom and back, so:

**2d = v × t → depth d = (v × t) ÷ 2**
topics.example:
**SONAR depth:** A ship sends an ultrasonic pulse towards the sea bed and receives the echo after 4 s. Speed of sound in sea water = 1531 m/s.

Total distance (down and back) = v × t = 1531 × 4 = 6124 m
Depth = 6124 ÷ 2 = **3062 m**
keyPoints: Infrasound < 20 Hz: elephants, whales, earthquakes
Ultrasound > 20 kHz: bats, dolphins; dogs can hear it
Uses: cleaning, detecting flaws in metals, ultrasonography
Bats use echolocation — ultrasonic squeaks and their echoes
SONAR = Sound Navigation And Ranging; transmitter + detector on a ship
Depth = speed × time ÷ 2

A region of a sound wave where particles are crowded together — high pressure and density.
A region of a sound wave where particles are spread apart — low pressure and density.
A wave in which particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels; sound is one.
The distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions; SI unit metre.
The number of complete oscillations per second; SI unit hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete oscillation; T = 1/ν.
The maximum disturbance of the medium from its mean value; it decides loudness.
How high or low a sound seems; it depends on frequency.
The feature that distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness; it depends on the waveform.
A reflected sound heard separately from the original, needing a gap of at least 0.1 s (reflector at least about 17 m away in air).
Persistence of sound in a large hall due to repeated reflections.
Sound of frequency above 20 kHz, beyond human hearing; used in SONAR, scans and cleaning.
Sound Navigation And Ranging — uses ultrasound echoes to find the depth of the sea and underwater objects.

formulas: v = λν (v speed of sound, λ wavelength, ν frequency)
ν = 1/T (ν frequency in Hz, T time period in s)
Echo / SONAR: distance to reflector (or depth) d = (v × t) ÷ 2, where t is the time for the sound to go and return
Minimum echo distance in air ≈ 346 × 0.1 ÷ 2 ≈ 17 m
commonMistakes: Thinking the air particles travel from the source to the ear — they only vibrate in place; energy travels.
Forgetting to divide by 2 in echo and SONAR problems — the sound goes to the reflector and back.
Mixing up loudness and pitch: loudness depends on amplitude, pitch depends on frequency.
Saying sound travels fastest in air — it is slowest in gases and fastest in solids.
Calling sound a transverse wave — sound in air is longitudinal.
Writing ν = T instead of ν = 1/T.
Confusing infrasound (below 20 Hz) with ultrasound (above 20 kHz).
revision: Sound is produced by vibrating objects (tuning fork, vocal cords).
Sound needs a medium; the bell-jar experiment shows it can't travel in a vacuum.
Sound travels as compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure).
Sound is a longitudinal wave; the medium vibrates in place while energy moves.
λ = distance between consecutive compressions; ν in Hz; T = 1/ν.
At 25 °C: aluminium 6420, steel 5960, glass 3980, sea water 1531, distilled water 1498, hydrogen 1284, air 346 m/s.
Speed of sound: solids > liquids > gases; increases with temperature.
Loudness ↔ amplitude (dB); pitch ↔ frequency; quality ↔ waveform.
Echo needs ≥ 0.1 s gap → reflector at least ≈ 17 m away.
Reverberation is reduced with curtains, carpets, fibreboard and cushioned seats.
Multiple reflection is used in megaphones, stethoscopes, sound boards and curved ceilings.
Infrasound < 20 Hz (elephants, whales); ultrasound > 20 kHz (bats, dolphins); SONAR depth = v × t ÷ 2.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an echo and reverberation?
faqs.a: An **echo** is a single, distinct repetition of a sound after it reflects from a far surface (at least about 17 m away), heard at least 0.1 s after the original. **Reverberation** is the lingering of sound in a large hall because of many repeated reflections that merge together, making the sound blurred.

faqs.q: What is the difference between loudness and pitch?
faqs.a: **Loudness** is how strong a sound seems and depends on **amplitude** (measured in dB). **Pitch** is how high or shrill a sound seems and depends on **frequency**. A mosquito's buzz is high-pitched but soft; a lion's roar is low-pitched but loud.

faqs.q: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
faqs.a: Both happen at the same moment, but light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s while sound in air travels at only about 346 m/s. So the light reaches us almost instantly and the sound arrives later.

faqs.q: Why do we divide by 2 in echo and SONAR calculations?
faqs.a: The measured time is for the sound to travel **to** the reflecting surface and **back**. So speed × time gives twice the distance; dividing by 2 gives the actual distance or depth.

faqs.q: Why is sound faster in solids than in gases?
faqs.a: In solids the particles are packed very closely and are strongly bound to each other, so a vibration is passed on very quickly. In gases the particles are far apart, so the disturbance takes longer to pass along.

faqs.q: What is the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves?
faqs.a: In a **longitudinal wave** (like sound) particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction of the wave, forming compressions and rarefactions. In a **transverse wave** (like ripples on water) particles vibrate **perpendicular** to the direction of the wave, forming crests and troughs.

quiz.q: In the bell-jar experiment, what happens as air is pumped out of the jar?
quiz.explain: Sound needs a medium; with less air, less sound reaches us, even though the bell keeps ringing.

quiz.q: In a sound wave, a region of high pressure and density is called a:
quiz.explain: Compressions are regions where particles are crowded together (high pressure).

quiz.q: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave because the particles of air:
options: Travel from the source to the listener
Vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave
quiz.explain: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel.

quiz.q: A sound wave has a time period of 0.002 s. Its frequency is:
A sound of frequency 346 Hz travels in air at 346 m/s. Its wavelength is:
In which medium does sound travel fastest (at 25 °C)?
quiz.explain: Aluminium, at 6420 m/s. Sound is fastest in solids.

quiz.q: The loudness of a sound depends mainly on its:
quiz.explain: Larger amplitude means more energy and a louder sound. Pitch depends on frequency.

quiz.q: A flute and a violin play the same note equally loudly, yet we can tell them apart. This is due to:
quiz.explain: Quality or timbre depends on the waveform and distinguishes sounds of the same pitch and loudness.

quiz.q: Taking the speed of sound in air as 346 m/s, the minimum distance of a reflector for a distinct echo is about:
quiz.explain: The echo must return after at least 0.1 s: 346 × 0.1 = 34.6 m for the round trip, so the reflector is 34.6 ÷ 2 ≈ 17.3 m away.

quiz.q: Which of these is used to reduce reverberation in a large hall?
quiz.explain: Soft, sound-absorbing materials reduce repeated reflections. Sound boards and megaphones use reflection instead.

quiz.q: Which of these animals uses ultrasound to find its way in the dark?
quiz.explain: Bats emit ultrasonic squeaks and use the echoes to locate obstacles and prey (echolocation). Elephants and whales use infrasound for long-distance calls.

quiz.q: A ship's SONAR receives the echo from the sea bed 2 s after sending the pulse. If sound travels at 1531 m/s in sea water, the depth is:
